items.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
items.summary: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.
items.content:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.

"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.

While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.

Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."

That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?

Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.

There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.

When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.

"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.

But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.

Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.

It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.

"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."

Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".

"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."

And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".

"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.

Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.

For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.

It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.

"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"

Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.

"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."

While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.

Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.

According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.

"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."

Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.

The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.

It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.

"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."

items.title: Ad Haiti, dove non si vota dal 2016, non si voterà nemmeno a dicembre
items.content:
Ad Haiti sono state rinviate a data da destinarsi le elezioni presidenziali e parlamentari che avrebbero dovuto tenersi a dicembre. Il rinvio era considerato molto probabile da tempo, soprattutto a causa della grave situazione di sicurezza: negli ultimi anni i gruppi criminali armati hanno esteso il loro controllo su gran parte della capitale Port-au-Prince e su altre zone del paese caraibico.

In diverse città non è stato possibile aprire centri per la registrazione degli elettori, e le minacce e i blocchi stradali imposti dalle bande hanno impedito di distribuire il materiale elettorale in alcune parti del paese.

Ad Haiti non si tengono elezioni dal 2016 e non c’è un presidente dal 2021, quando Jovenel Moïse fu assassinato a casa sua. Da allora il paese è stato governato da una serie di autorità provvisorie . Nel 2024 era stato istituito un Consiglio presidenziale di transizione, che avrebbe dovuto assicurare una certa stabilità e organizzare nuove elezioni, ma il suo mandato è terminato lo scorso 7 febbraio senza che fosse riuscito a farlo. Il potere esecutivo è quindi passato al Consiglio dei ministri guidato dal primo ministro Alix Didier Fils-Aimé. Le elezioni sono considerate uno dei passaggi fondamentali per riportare ad Haiti un governo democraticamente eletto.

items.title: Pornhub returns to Australia but only for adults with Apple devices
items.summary: The world's most popular porn site went dark in March in Australia due to age verification laws.
items.content:
Pornhub has returned to Australia, eight months after it went dark due to age verification laws, but only adults with Apple devices will be able to access the site.

On Wednesday, parent company Aylo said it was restoring access for "eligible adult users in Australia" who have "confirmed their age through Apple's Australian age-verification process".

The world's biggest porn site left the Australian market in March, saying new laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 would not protect children and "instead creates harms relating to data privacy" and exposure to content on non-compliant platforms.

Apple recently introduced new age checks in Australia, following a rollout in the UK.

In March, Australia introduced stricter laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 in order to access adult content such as porn, R-rated video games and sexually explicit AI chatbots.

The country's online safety regulator said the changes would protect children from harmful content and platforms would be fined for breaches.

Critics said there would be issues with data privacy and users finding ways to trick age-verification technologies such as facial recognition, digital IDs and credit card details.

Aylo said it was returning to Australia as Apple has "set a benchmark" by setting default child safety features on all devices unless owners confirmed they are adults.

This, in effect, makes "every phone or tablet kid-safe as a starting point," it said.

"For years, Aylo has advocated for device-based age verification as the most effective and privacy-protecting approach to help prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content online," said Aylo's vice-president of brand and community Alex Kekesi.

Australians with Apple devices that have been "age-verified" will be "served a standard adult users experience", she said.

Apple users can prove they are over 18 using a credit card, their passport, a driver's license or a government-issued ID.

Kekesi added that having devices with child safety features as a default meant adults don't have to "surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites".

It also limits the usefulness of virtual private networks (VPNs) to circumvent age-verification technologies, she said.

VPNs are commonly used to trick a site into thinking a user is logging on from another country, giving the user access to the site.

items.title: Hackers obtain counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large services
items.summary: Article URL: https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/hackers-obtain-counterfeit-tls-certificates-for-google-and-other-large-services/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49988230 Points: 33 # Comments: 5
items.content:
Attackers hijacked three top-level domains and used their control to mint counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large organizations, Google said Tuesday.

The attackers launched a series of attacks on the .gh, .sl, and .as country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) and then modified authoritative DNS records for selected domains within those namespaces. By controlling those DNS records, the attackers were able to pass automated domain control validation checks and obtain unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Google said it updated Chrome to block all certificates it identified as unauthorized, and worked with the issuing certification authorities to ensure the unauthorized certificates for Google properties were revoked.

TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials that underpin authentication and encryption protections for websites, mail servers, and other Internet infrastructure. These x.509 certificates use a digital signature to bind a domain name such as google.com to a public key. The public key is publicly available, while the private key is held only by the website operator. When a connection shows that the keys match, the visiting party knows it’s connected to the authentic site rather than an impostor. Possession of unauthorized certificates allows attackers to cryptographically impersonate the affected infrastructure.

Google didn’t identify the affected domains it owns or name any of the other organizations whose domains were affected. While noting that Chrome users do not need to take any action to be protected, Google cautioned domain owners not to rely solely on browser-side interventions to protect their users. The company is advising domain owners to monitor certificate transparency logs for unexpected certificate issuance across their domains and to publish restrictive Certification Authority Authorization DNS records to prevent attackers from reusing cached validation data after DNS control is restored.

“While Chrome took steps during these incidents to identify and block suspected unauthorized certificates across the affected ccTLDs, browser-side intervention should not be relied on to protect your users,” Google said . “Due to the complexity of DNS hijacks, we cannot guarantee that our analysis identified every affected domain, nor do Chrome interventions reliably protect non-Chrome users.”

It’s not immediately clear what the other affected organizations are, how many unauthorized certificates were issued, or if all of them, except for those for Google domains, have been blocked. The process for officially revoking certificates is slow and cumbersome, so browser makers have devised quicker methods to block specific certificates at the browser level. With all known unauthorized certificates now blocked, the risk is mitigated, but as Google noted, any certificates that remain undiscovered pose a threat.

Google noted that the incident didn’t involve the compromise of the infrastructure of any of the affected domain owners and that certificate authorities followed all requirements. With control of the three ccTLDs, the attackers were able to change the IP addresses of a selected list of websites. With the ability to send and receive traffic on those sites, the attackers were able to modify authoritative DNS records and nameserver delegations for selected domains, allowing them to pass industry validation checks requiring an applicant to prove control of the domain.

This isn’t the first time threat actors have obtained unauthorized certificates. A 2011 hack of Netherlands-based certificate authority DigiNotar allowed attackers to mint counterfeit certificates for Google.com and more than 200 other high-traffic domains. The certificates were used against at least 300,000 people with ties to Iran as they browsed the sites impersonated by the forged certificates. There have been many similar incidents since, most often through failures by certificate authorities but also domain holders .

items.title: Former Australian bishop jailed for sexually abusing young men
items.summary: The former Bishop of Broome is one of the most senior Catholic clerics in the world to face sex abuse charges.
items.content:
Former Australian bishop Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men during his time as a Catholic cleric.

Saunders - who resigned as Bishop of Broome when first accused of wrongdoing in 2020 - was found guilty of one charge of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault in August.

The 76-year-old was on Wednesday sentenced to six and a half years in prison, but will be eligible for release on parole in February 2031.

He is one of the most senior Catholic leaders in the world to face sex abuse charges.

His trial in the state of Western Australia heard Saunders systematically groomed the two young men, inviting them to "shirts-off" gatherings and plying them with alcohol, often using church funds and church-owned properties to do so.

He was convicted of kissing and molesting the men between 2010 and 2019, and in one instance forcing oral sex on one of them.

In a victim impact statement provided to the court, that young man said he still struggled to talk about what had happened.

"I was a toy that he was using," the victim wrote. "My head is pounding now, I'm in so much pain."

"I trusted him. I thought he wanted me to be a better person."

During the trial several child sex abuse charges were discarded, and Saunders was acquitted by the jury of alleged offences against a third young man.

First ordained in 1976, Saunders spent most of his career in the remote Kimberley region in the nation's north-west corner, and was appointed Bishop of Broome in 1996.

The diocese stretches about 770,000 sq km (297,000 sq miles) - an area roughly the size of Turkey - and encompasses some of the most remote parts of the country.

District Court Judge Martin Flynn said Saunders had professed to be an advocate for young Aboriginal men, but instead misused his authority and exploited their vulnerability.

He had "disregarded the dignity" of his victims and caused them lasting harm.

In a statement, Archbishop of Perth Timothy Costelloe said the men who had come forward had shown great courage and resilience in pursuing justice.

"We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the church," he said.

"No court sentence can undo the suffering that has been caused or restore all that each person has lost."

The accusations were first aired in 2020, but the initial police investigation that followed was closed without charge.

However after a historic inquiry was ordered by the Pope, police began a new investigation.

Costelloe has previously said the church's investigation into Saunders - paused when police resumed theirs - will restart.

The church is under pressure to strip Saunders of his remaining title and ministry powers, a decision the Archbishop said would be determined by Rome.

Only a handful of "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" - meaning "You Are the Light of the World" in Latin - inquiries have been undertaken around the world.

The investigations are commissioned by the pontiff and were introduced in 2019 to combat sexual abuse and hold bishops and other high-ranking Catholic Church officials accountable for their actions.

Aside from the late Cardinal George Pell, who was jailed and then acquitted, Saunders is the most senior Catholic official in the country to be charged with sex offences.

items.title: Calling It Quits on ServerFault
items.summary: Article URL: https://sysadmin1138.net/mt/blog/2026/10/calling-it-quits-on-serverfault.shtml Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49988142 Points: 61 # Comments: 28
items.content:
It's time to be done after just over 15 years of moderator work. I was elected in the very first community election in January and February of 2011 , and by now I'm quite possibly in the top five for longest serving community moderators on the original trilogy sites of StackOverflow, ServerFault, and SuperUser. I could check, but I'm not motivated. SF has always been the one I worked with and for. 15 years, and I've learned so much about moderation and online technical communities.

The early years of ServerFault were vastly more fractious than the site has been in the last 10, and taught me so much. One particularly vivid example was seeing the toxic reverberations between users from different countries and how they handle escalation of conflict. A particularly volatile mix were the Russian speakers and the folk from the United Kingdom (this was before Brexit), where the very British snide (a plus-one or two escalation from just asking questions, the next step was ad hominem attacks) was taken as an invitation to fight by the Russian speakers (whose plus-one escalation typically was ad hominem attacks, which means the brits saw this as escalation and moved on to flame war), both of which deeply and horribly offended US-based users for whom both were plus-two or plus-three escalations, definitely not a plus one. These flame wars proved the need for moderator coverage during US night time, which has been a factor in every election after mine. It also drove the feature to lock posts to get folk to cool down.

However, the site has been in decline for a long time. The peak for question asking was in 2011-2012, with a change to Google algorithms in 2013 causing a sizable drop in traffic in late 2013 to 2014. The long slow decline started in 2016, and in recent months we're getting 2-3 questions a day. The moderator flag queue mostly is dealing with spam. Even the Suggested Edit queue, once a great place to farm reputation by fixing other's grammar and formatting mistakes, has slowed down enough that two people can keep it from getting clogged.

The biggest moderator thing I was involved in the last few years were StackExchange-wide spam campaigns that also targeted ServerFault. Manual remediation was required until StackExchange could figure out technical fixes, and it was a bad 12 months there. SuperUser got it way worse than we did, but our downvote and site traffic numbers have clear spikes 2x and 3x above our baseline traffic during the spam surges. There were a few months in there where I spent my evenings watching the new-user creations and spam-banning and deleting in real time. The new technical measures have made that sort of coordinated spam campaign much harder to execute, and is working.

We haven't had a major debate about policy on ServerFault in a long, long time. StackExchange as a whole regularly has major debates, but ServerFault in specific hasn't.

In the last few months the Suggested Edit queue has been barely active, which is the signal that it's time. I'm out as of the end of the year. It's now up to the community to decide if it's worth replacing me.

items.title: Il grande sgombero italiano di cui nessuno parla
items.summary: A Ferrara un edificio è stato sgomberato otto mesi fa e più di cinquecento persone sono rimaste per strada. Un caso simile a quello dello Spin Time di Roma, ma che ha attirato meno l’attenzione Leggi
items.content:
Quando Amara Sacko ha capito che non sarebbe tornato in tempi brevi a casa erano passati appena sette giorni dall’incendio. Non riusciva a lavorare, a dormire. Non pensava ad altro che allo sgombero. Gli amici gli mandavano gli screenshot dei commenti sotto le notizie sul cosiddetto grattacielo di Ferrara, il palazzo dove aveva comprato un appartamento e da cui era stato costretto ad andarsene. Erano commenti razzisti, auguravano il peggio agli abitanti del palazzo in larga parte stranieri. Ha dovuto dire agli amici di non mostrarglieli più, perché non riusciva a leggerli. Ha anche pensato di tornare nel suo paese di origine, la Guinea.

Sacko, 29 anni, è arrivato in Italia nel 2018, lavora come facchino con un contratto a tempo indeterminato e fino all’11 gennaio 2026 aveva una casa. L’aveva comprata con un mutuo, il perito della banca che aveva verificato l’agibilità dell’appartamento e dato il via libera all’acquisto. La rata stabilita era di 316 euro al mese, per trent’anni. Con uno stipendio di 1.400 euro, Sacko pensava di aver fatto un buon investimento, che gli avrebbe risparmiato le lunghe ricerche per l’affitto di un posto dove vivere. Ma otto mesi dopo lo sgombero, paga ancora, per evitare ripetizione il mutuo di una casa in cui non può più abitare e le autorità continuano a non dargli risposte sul futuro.

Il grattacielo in cui abitava si trova vicino alla stazione ferroviaria di Ferrara. È un complesso formato da tre torri, costruito alla fine degli anni cinquanta per offrire abitazioni a basso costo al ceto medio. Doveva essere una costruzione all’avanguardia per la città, ma ha finito per diventare un ghetto, in cui nel tempo si sono trasferiti soprattutto lavoratori e lavoratrici stranieri per i costi contenuti delle abitazioni.

Negli ultimi anni la zona è stata al centro di una campagna di demonizzazione dei politici locali, che l’hanno rappresentata come una specie di buco nero: un quartiero di degrado, spaccio, prostituzione e criminalità, contrapposta alla città rinascimentale con la sua bellezza eterna.

La notte dell’11 gennaio è scoppiato un incendio nel vano dei contatori della torre B. Il fumo ha invaso rapidamente l’edificio e sono arrivati i vigili del fuoco, che hanno chiesto agli abitanti di lasciare le loro case.

Tutti pensavano che sarebbe stato un intervento temporaneo per sedare l’incendio e mettere in sicurezza l’immobile. Invece l’evacuazione è diventata uno sgombero permanente, come’è successo nel luglio 2026 agli abitanti dello Spin Time di Roma . Con una differenza: gli abitanti del grattacielo di Ferrara in molti casi erano proprietari degli appartamenti. Quasi la metà di loro erano piccoli proprietari stranieri come Sacko.

Dopo l’incendio la torre B è stata dichiarata inagibile. Dieci giorni dopo, il comune di Ferrara ha disposto lo sgombero anche delle torri A e C: circa 250 persone hanno avuto quindici giorni per lasciare gli appartamenti e circa cinquecento sono rimaste senza case. Gli impianti della struttura erano da rifare, secondo i rilievi dei vigili del fuoco, e non c’erano le condizioni di sicurezza per permettere agli abitanti di rientrare nei loro appartamenti. Alcune parti comuni dei condomini non risultavano a norma, così come una parte degli appartamenti.

A differenza dello Spin Time, l’amministrazione comunale di Ferrara, contraria alla presenza di immigrati in città, non è intervenuta per trovare una soluzione, ma ha offerto una sistemazione temporanea solo per i casi più vulnerabili: persone malate o con disabilità e famiglie con minori.

Nelle prime settimane dopo lo sgombero, una parte degli abitanti è stata ospitata dall’associazione viale K e successivamente e temporaneamente nell’ex convento di San Bartolo gestito dalla Caritas diocesana, un’ottantina di persone in alberghi e bed and breakfast pagati dal comune. Ma dal 30 giugno non sono più a disposizione i rifugi di emergenza, anche se alcuni sono ancora ospitati negli hotel e nei bed and breakfast. Altri hanno trovato una sistemazione da amici o parenti, alcuni hanno cercato un’altra casa in affitto.

Amara Sacko ha affittato un posto letto nella casa di un conoscente, in un paese vicino a Ferrara, ma tra il mutuo della casa inagibile e questa nuova spesa non arriva a fine mese. “È una situazione molto difficile”, sottolinea. Ha sempre creduto che lavorando avrebbe trovato una stabilità, ma non aveva considerato la possibilità di uno sgombero.

In questa situazione ha anche dovuto affrontare la sensazione di sentirsi un eterno straniero. “Ci dicono che siamo tutti mafiosi o criminali, solo perché siamo stranieri”, racconta, ripensando alle parole e ai commenti che ha letto nelle settimane successive allo sgombero. “Per noi continua a essere complicato anche farci affittare casa”.

Poi ha incontrato i volontari di Cittadini del mondo e molti altri ferraresi che si sono mobilitati per gli abitanti del grattacielo. Ha partecipato a delle riunioni. All’inizio si è tenuto in disparte, ascoltava. Poi gli hanno chiesto se voleva dire la sua e allora ha cominciato a prendere parola anche per quelli che non avevano più voglia di farlo. “Per tanti di noi è una causa persa. E fa molto male”, racconta.

Otto mesi dopo “è ancora tutto fermo”, racconta Carola Peverati, di Cittadini del mondo, un’associazione multiculturale che ha una sede vicino al grattacielo e che in questi mesi ha assistito gli ex abitanti.

“Le persone più vulnerabili, quelle che avevano disabilità o figli minorenni sono in situazioni di emergenza talmente gravi che stanno lasciando la città”, racconta Peverati. “Se ti mettono in una stanza in cui non c’è neanche un armadio, quanto puoi resistere?”.

In alcuni casi le famiglie sono state divise: le donne con i figli in strutture destinate all’accoglienza, gli uomini in altre sistemazioni temporanee per senza dimora. “C’è un uomo con disabilità che vive con il figlio di undici anni in una stanza d’albergo vicino alla stazione, senza neanche un armadio”, racconta l’attivista. Secondo la ricostruzione dell’associazione, il comune di Ferrara ha trovato una sistemazione d’emergenza per circa 78 persone. Gli ospiti contribuiscono alle spese in base al proprio reddito, mentre l’amministrazione paga il resto.

“Assegnargli case d’emergenza, invece di pagargli gli alberghi, costerebbe molto meno”, osserva Peverati . Il mercato degli affitti, intanto, non ha offerto una soluzione. “È impossibile, una casa in affitto non gliela dà nessuno”, dice Peverati. Tra i motivi ci sono la diffidenza nei confronti degli stranieri e la domanda di posti letto degli studenti, particolarmente forte in una città universitaria, racconta l’attivista. A questo si aggiungono gli affitti brevi legati agli eventi e ai concerti.

“I piccoli proprietari del grattacielo sono disperati perché devono continuare a pagare il mutuo”, dice Peverati. “Se diventano insolventi dopo un certo periodo non possono più prendere un prestito da nessuna parte”.

Negli ultimi mesi è emerso un debito condominiale ingente. Una parte della cifra, secondo la documentazione esaminata dagli abitanti, sarebbe legata però a insoluti di singoli inquilini e ai lavori di messa a norma delle proprietà.

L’amministratore del condominio si è dimesso e ora dovrà essere nominato un nuovo amministratore. Nel frattempo gli interventi necessari per la sicurezza dell’edificio non sono ancora partiti. “Secondo i condomini, gli appartamenti non a norma sarebbero 38 su 184. A loro si aggiungerebbero alcune criticità nelle parti comuni”, spiega Peverati.

All’inizio di ottobre alcuni sgomberati hanno ricevuto dal comune la notizia che alcune case di emergenza sarebbero pronte ad accogliere alcuni di loro, ma le informazioni non sono state chiare. L’assessora alle politiche sociali e abitative Cristina Coletti non ha risposto alla nostra richiesta di maggiori informazioni e di un commento.

Ona Shuhui Ouyang ha comprato la sua casa il 10 ottobre 2023. Anche lei aveva fatto tutto quello che le era stato richiesto prima dell’acquisto. Aveva domandato alla vecchia proprietaria la documentazione sull’agibilità. Un ingegnere era andato al comune di Ferrara per ottenere il certificato. Poi era arrivata la banca, con la perizia necessaria per il mutuo.

“Il perito è andato a casa per vedere se era tutto a posto, se valeva quella cifra. Dopo qualche giorno abbiamo ricevuto il messaggio che la perizia era completata. La banca ha detto che andava tutto bene e mi ha concesso il mutuo”, racconta la ragazza, che lavora come apprendista nel settore tessile e ha una disabilità del 67 per cento. Per comprare quell’appartamento ha fatto i conti con uno stipendio di circa mille euro al mese e una rata del mutuo di 250 euro. Ha messo da parte i soldi per rifare l’impianto elettrico e ha pagato un tecnico per sistemarlo. Ha partecipato alle assemblee condominiali, votato per i lavori, pagato le spese straordinarie.

Poi, pochi anni dopo ha perso la casa. Ora condivide una sistemazione d’emergenza con altre donne, ma le stanno facendo pressione perché trovi un’altra soluzione in autonomia. Ha fatto domanda per una casa popolare, ma nonostante la sua disabilità non ha ottenuto risposta. “Se il comune conosceva questi problemi, come ha potuto rilasciare l’agibilità alle persone che compravano, vendevano o affittavano gli appartamenti?”, chiede.

items.title: Rome is doing far more for Ukraine than it admits
items.summary: Italy’s military aid to Ukraine has been shrouded in secrecy since 2022, when Mario Draghi’s government imposed a strict veil of silence that Giorgia Meloni has maintained. Official statements focus on humanitarian assistance, but behind the scenes, contribution goes much further
items.content:
Italy delivers, but doesn't talk about it. Piecing together the country’s contribution to Ukraine’s resistance is difficult because its military assistance has been shrouded in strict secrecy from the very beginning.

The Kiel Institute’s Top 20 Military Aid Donors to Ukraine ranking places Italy 13th in 2025, with contributions approaching €1 billion. The actual figure is believed to be higher, concealed behind a wall of silence imposed by Mario Draghi’s government in spring 2022 and maintained by Giorgia Meloni’s administration.

While secrecy was common among other European countries, including France, during the first months of the invasion, it subsequently became an important political tool for Italy’s right-wing government. It has allowed the prime minister to maintain firm support for Kyiv despite divisions within public opinion and her own governing coalition.

The coalition includes Lega (The League), the party led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, which opposes supplying weapons to Kyiv and has longstanding ties to Moscow. In the past, it signed a cooperation agreement with Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party.

There are deep divisions within the opposition, too. The populist Five Star Movement – Movimento Cinque Stelle – opposes arms deliveries, as does part of the electorate of the left-wing Partito Democratico (Democratic Party).

Further complicating the picture is the new far-right party Futuro Nazionale, founded by former paratrooper general Roberto Vannacci, which has adopted a strongly pro-Russian stance. Polls put its support at more than 8% ahead of elections scheduled for autumn next year.

In their official statements, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Defence Minister Guido Crosetto focus exclusively on humanitarian assistance, such as electricity generators, or funding to rebuild hospitals and schools.

Shipments of military equipment, by contrast, are authorised by government decrees, and only COPASIR, the parliamentary committee overseeing Italy’s intelligence services, is informed of exactly what is being transferred. In public statements, the emphasis is invariably on the “defensive” nature of the equipment.

In fact, Mario Draghi also authorised the supply of offensive weapons. Some were Cold War-era systems refurbished with US funding: 155mm artillery pieces, M109 self-propelled howitzers of the same calibre, heavy mortars, machine guns, Skyguard-Aspide anti-aircraft missile batteries and large quantities of ammunition.

These were supplemented, in limited numbers, by modern weapons drawn from the Italian Army’s own arsenal, including multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS), PzH 2000 self-propelled howitzers and shoulder-fired Stinger missiles.

Giorgia Meloni has continued along the same lines. Older equipment, including M113 tracked armoured personnel carriers, Centauro armoured vehicles equipped with 105mm guns, Puma armoured vehicles and Lince military vehicles, has been supplied alongside two expensive SAMP/T surface-to-air missile batteries, one provided jointly with France, as well as radar systems and electronic countermeasure equipment.

Cooperation between Italian and Ukrainian defence companies has also been encouraged. Leonardo has opened a local subsidiary, while Fincantieri is designing a protective network for the port of Odesa and participating in a joint European drone development programme. Rheinmetall Italia is manufacturing anti-aircraft guns for Kyiv with German funding.

By October, Rome will have to honour its joint commitment with Paris to equip Ukraine with a missile defence shield. Plans include the sale of radar systems and four next-generation SAMP/T NG batteries, the delivery of Aster 30 interceptor missiles and their subsequent production under licence.

The entire project is to be financed through European funds, with the aim of providing an alternative to American Patriot systems, which the Trump administration is no longer supplying.

The Zelensky administration is particularly appreciative of Italy’s diplomatic efforts in Brussels, which it regards as crucial to overcoming vetoes blocking Ukraine’s EU accession process and the approval of vital funding.

Divisions within Italy’s governing coalition and tensions with the Élysée Palace have, however, limited Rome’s participation in other initiatives.

In the summer of 2025, Italy initially joined the “Coalition of the Willing”, launched by London and Paris to provide security guarantees for Kyiv in the event of an agreement with Russia.

Defence Minister Crosetto and Foreign Minister Tajani had raised the possibility of deploying Italian forces to clear mines on land and at sea. But the proposal was abruptly shelved. Since then, the government has ruled out sending troops even in the event of a peace agreement.

items.title: Inside Moto Guzzi’s new home: celebrating its heritage, looking to the future
items.summary: Designed by American architect Greg Lynn, the cutting-edge complex brings together manufacturing, architecture and design, opening a new chapter in the Italian motorcycle maker’s history
items.content:
The legendary Eagle is looking to the future. And it's starting again from where it all began, exactly 105 years ago, on the eastern shore of Lake Como. Founded in 1921 by friends Carlo Guzzi and Giorgio Parodi, Moto Guzzi has unveiled a completely redesigned headquarters in Mandello del Lario.

Conceived by visionary American architect Greg Lynn, the new complex aims to become a global benchmark for technological innovation in the motorcycle industry. For the Piaggio Group, the ambition is to carry Moto Guzzi’s heritage into the future, opening a new chapter in the relationship between factory, museum and the surrounding area.

Mandello is no longer simply the town where the company is based: it is set to become an essential part of the Moto Guzzi experience.

Five years of work and an investment of more than €50 million have produced a futuristic, multifunctional complex, developed entirely within the historic site where Moto Guzzi has always manufactured its motorcycles. The design brings together existing buildings and new structures, indoor spaces and areas open to the surrounding landscape, alongside expanded, increasingly automated production facilities. The ambition is also to turn the site into a hub for culture, creativity and knowledge.

“Moto Guzzi is unlike any other factory I’ve ever saw, thanks to its extraordinary location between the lake and the mountains. The first time I visited the museum, I found myself looking at the large empty space that was to become part of the redevelopment project. I thought that if visitors could enter through the legendary red gate on Via Parodi, which marks the entrance to the site, reach this square and, from there, look inside the new warehouse, the engine factory, the assembly line and the testing and restoration buildings without disrupting production, it would add tremendous value to the entire complex,” explains Greg Lynn, the internationally renowned architect and professor at UCLA in Los Angeles, who is also CEO and co-founder of Piaggio Fast Forward, the Piaggio Group’s robotics and lightweight mobility division.

“I’ve visited Lake Como many times as a tourist, and every time I return, I try to discover somewhere new. It’s exactly what riders do, driven by the desire to seek out hidden gems.”

Moto Guzzi’s new home is a factory open to the public, a place where the Eagle’s heritage is created, preserved and shared. Here, manufacturing is more than an industrial operation: it tells the story of the brand’s identity, which is why the production process has been made visible to visitors.

The industrial complex includes 5,500 square metres of new buildings, allowing production capacity to increase by more than 30,000 vehicles a year. Its state-of-the-art assembly lines also incorporate innovative technology: motorcycles are transported to their final testing stations by kilo robots, designed and manufactured in Boston by Piaggio Fast Forward. The production facilities themselves become part of the visitor experience, offering a glimpse of the brand’s continuing commitment to innovation and technological development.

Next to the factory, the new museum houses Moto Guzzi’s extensive heritage, telling the company’s story through invention, engineering and innovation. Covering 3,000 square metres, the building draws inspiration from the technical language and distinctive details of motorcycles. Large circular openings, for example, evoke motorcycle wheels, translating the shapes, materials and finishes of the machines into architectural features and creating a direct connection between the building and the products it celebrates.

The company’s history unfolds through more than 160 restored motorcycles, organised into thematic sections ranging from travel to racing. Together, they trace not only the evolution of motorcycle technology but also changes in Italian society, design and popular culture.

Over the decades, Moto Guzzi has specialised in racing prototypes and the mass production of motorcycles and three-wheeled vehicles, some of which were supplied to military forces in Italy and abroad. Its motorcycles have also featured prominently in Italian cinema, becoming part of the visual identity of a country on the move. From classic Italian comedies such as An American in Rome (1954) and The Traffic Policeman (1960) to Federico Fellini’s Roma (1972) and City of Women (1980), Moto Guzzi has left its mark on the silver screen.

Among the models on display are the Airone, Italy’s most popular mid-sized motorcycle between 1939 and 1957; the Falcone, the dream machine of motorcyclists in the 1950s; the Motoleggera 65, affectionately known as the “Guzzino”; the Galletto; and the enduringly desirable California. Each became a symbol of style and innovation, appealing to an international audience far beyond motorcycle enthusiasts.

The exhibition design for the new museum is by UniFor, which has translated Moto Guzzi’s identity into a coherent, flexible and entirely bespoke display system. Overseeing every stage from design and engineering to production, the company has created a series of custom-made solutions integrated into the architecture.

These include platforms and plinths of different shapes and sizes for displaying the motorcycles, as well as showcases, display units and supports for memorabilia, accessories, clothing and scale models. Components from the X Shelving system by Foster + Partners and the CF system by Dante Bonuccelli have been used to display the helmet collection and archival materials. The lounge areas feature pieces from the PRINCIPLES collection, designed by OMA.

The redesigned headquarters also includes outdoor event spaces, the restored historic wind tunnel at the foot of the mountain, an auditorium, a café, a shop and dedicated visitor routes. Altogether, 4,200 square metres have been allocated to new public and multifunctional facilities.

UniFor’s contribution extends beyond the museum to the reception areas and visitor facilities, with specially designed furnishings for the café, merchandising area and the Moto Guzzi Historic Register. The company has also furnished the photographic archive, prototype storage areas and several operational spaces, where Jean Nouvel’s LessLess tables, drawer units and cabinets have been installed.

In the waiting areas, Molteni&C has added a further touch of Italian design with Paul sofas by Vincent Van Duysen.

items.title: Mancini’s new Italy: a team shaped by immigration
items.summary: The coach is calling up very young second-generation players as well as Italians playing for clubs abroad
items.content:
Italy’s national football team finally appears to have entered a new era. After failing to qualify for three consecutive World Cups — in 2018, 2022 and 2026, the latest disappointment coming only a few months ago — "the Azzurri” have brought Roberto Mancini back as head coach.

Mancini led Italy to the European Championship title in 2021 before leaving the national team after being lured by a huge financial offer to take charge of Saudi Arabia. That experience ended earlier than planned, before his contract was due to expire.Once free of other commitments, Mancini was able to accept an offer from the new president of the Italian Football Federation, Giovanni Malagò.

The optimism and hopes of Italian supporters had, in fact, suffered a sharp setback the previous week after Italy’s heavy defeat in Rome in their Nations League opener against Belgium. It was almost a footballing lesson.

But just a few days later, the Azzurri bounced back in Turkey with an emphatic 4-1 victory, laying the foundations for renewed optimism.

Those positive thoughts were further justified by the significant 1-1 draw away to France on Friday night. France are one of the strongest teams in the world and have long been an example of a multicultural national side — something the Azzurri, as we shall see, are also becoming.

After falling behind, Mancini’s Italy fought back to equalise and even came close to winning the game in the closing stages. It was an important step forward in the attempt to rebuild an entire sporting system that is in deep crisis.

Mancini has also conceived his new national team as an opportunity for young players making their debuts, such as the Esposito brothers — although Pio had already played for Italy, he had rarely started as the central striker — as well as defender Kayode and centre-back Scalvini.

These are players looking to the future, and Mancini has put his faith in them. But perhaps the most important development is the mentality the national team already seems to have acquired: attacking football and an attempt to take control of every game.

Rather than adopting the passive approach that fear of stronger opponents can sometimes encourage, there is a kind of youthful boldness that casts fear aside and allows the players to look any opponent straight in the eye.

That does not necessarily mean winning every game. It means trying to. And that in itself is a major achievement.

The new era for the Italian national team has two main competitive objectives: qualifying for the next European Championship and World Cup. The Nations League is a necessary step if Italy are to remain in the competition’s top tier, but it should also be viewed as part of a longer-term project: reviving the Azzurri set-up — not just the senior team but the youth sides as well — is the foundation for any future success.

After watching three World Cups from the sidelines, Italian football urgently needs to reclaim the place its sporting history has traditionally afforded it: four World Cups, in 1934, 1938, 1982 and 2006, the most recent of them 20 years ago. That is a very long time.

The task of restoring Italy to a leading role rests above all on Roberto Mancini’s ideas and decisions. An outstanding player himself in the 1980s and 1990s, Mancini knows better than most that winning depends not only on physical strength but also on technique, class and attitude on the pitch.

The excellent draw in Paris against France may prove to be the starting point for a journey that has only just begun —a promising path towards the future.

The new-look national team also tells the story of a changing Italy from a social perspective: an Italy of the children and grandchildren of foreigners who emigrated there years or even decades ago.

These are the second and third generations, made up largely of young people born in Italy but still growing up in unequal circumstances, from families who may or may not have regular residence permits.

Either way, this is now part of the country’s reality, visible in schools from early childhood — from the ages of three to six — as well as in the workplace and in sport. Football, following other sports, is now catching up.

In the national team, Kean, Kayode and Doumbia are examples: Black athletes who are, naturally, Italian. They can be seen as genuine trailblazers, following in the footsteps of one of the first, Mario Balotelli, who unfortunately also had to contend with serious episodes of racism.

Mancini is not limiting his search for potential call-ups to players competing in Serie A, Italy’s top professional division. For these Nations League matches, he has called up Kayode, who plays for Brentford in England, and Doumbia, who is with Sporting Lisbon in Portugal. Keeping an eye on what is happening in other European leagues broadens Mancini’s options, particularly because some players who struggled for opportunities in Serie A have become regular starters abroad.

Kayode, for example, was not considered good enough first by Juventus and then by Fiorentina, but has established himself as a first-team player outside Italy.

It is also a way of finally making Italian football a little more international and less closed off to the experiences young players can have by leaving Italy. In that sense, their stories mirror those of many Italian students and workers, who find greater opportunities and a wider range of experiences beyond Italy’s borders.

That is why it is worth remembering that sport also reflects everyday life — and the society that produces it.

items.title: Un pappagallo dopato che si specchia
items.summary: Quando vogliamo definire e descrivere l’ultimo prodotto delle tecnologie digitali non riusciamo a fare meno di metafore più o meno indovinate, a partire da quella che si è diffusa di più: “intelligenza artificiale” Leggi
items.content:
Il 31 agosto 1955 quattro ricercatori statunitensi, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester e Claude Shannon, firmarono la proposta per un seminario estivo da tenere l’anno dopo al Dartmouth college, nel New Hampshire. Nel titolo del seminario c’era un’espressione nuova: “intelligenza artificiale”.

Settantuno anni dopo possiamo dire che l’espressione è particolarmente indovinata e, allo stesso tempo, che ci ha creato un sacco di problemi. È stata anche la prima metafora di una lunga serie di modi di dire che usiamo per riferirci a queste tecnologie.

Se vogliamo essere rigorosi, alcune di queste espressioni sono metafore in senso stretto, come quando si parla di “allucinazioni” dei modelli linguistici. Altre, invece, sono analogie. Ma il linguista George Lakoff e il filosofo Mark Johnson, in Metafora e vita quotidiana , ci hanno tolto dall’imbarazzo e le hanno riunite sotto l’etichetta “metafore concettuali”. Cioè, parole che usiamo per avvicinarci alla comprensione di una cosa attraverso un’altra cosa che conosciamo meglio.

Il problema delle metafore concettuali è che tendono a concentrarsi su una parte del funzionamento delle ia lasciando da parte tutto il resto. Qui ho provato a elencare in maniera critica le più diffuse.

È una delle espressioni più famose: nasce da un articolo del 2021 firmato da Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major e Margaret Mitchell. Funziona molto bene perché ricorda il meccanismo alla base dei large language model ( llm ): questi sistemi producono sequenze di parole plausibili in base alla probabilità, senza garanzie di corrispondenza con il mondo.

Qualcuno potrebbe obiettare che anche quel che dice una persona non dà nessuna garanzia di corrispondenza con il mondo, ma per ora lasciamo da parte queste considerazioni.

L’articolo, pubblicato online con l’emoji del pappagallo 列 nel titolo, parlava anche dei costi ambientali di modelli sempre più grandi e dei pregiudizi contenuti nei dati. Questa parte, purtroppo, si è persa quasi del tutto per strada, fagocitata dalla metafora stessa. Anni dopo, Emily Bender ha dovuto fare alcune precisazioni sul suo lavoro lamentando proprio questa dinamica, che ha fatto parecchi danni.

Nel frattempo, però, il pappagallo è diventato una metafora sempre più stretta: i comportamenti emergenti e le rappresentazioni interne ai modelli individuate da chi fa ricerca la rendono sempre meno vera. “È solo un pappagallo stocastico” (o “è solo statistica”) è diventata una frase per chiudere le discussioni proprio quando bisognerebbe aprirle, visto che con questi strumenti si possono fare tantissime cose.

I pappagalli veri, tra l’altro, ne escono particolarmente maltrattati visto che sono animali sociali e piuttosto intelligenti.

“Allucinazione” dà un nome a un’esperienza che chiunque abbia usato un chatbot riconosce: la risposta falsa detta con sicurezza. Ma, se pensiamo al suo significato originario, ci suggerisce anche una mente che percepisce le cose in maniera alterata e ci fa pensare che l’errore dipenda da un guasto del sistema.

Eppure le risposte giuste degli llm e quelle sbagliate sono il frutto dello stesso identico meccanismo.

Nel 2024 i filosofi Michael Townsen Hicks, James Humphries e Joe Slater hanno proposto un’alternativa: i chatbot producono stronzate nel senso descritto da Harry Frankfurt in Stronzate. Un saggio filosofico . Significa che i discorsi delle macchine sono indifferenti alla verità. È un’immagine più precisa del loro funzionamento.

Anche questa, però, ha almeno due problemi: prima di tutto, attribuisce un atteggiamento – l’indifferenza – a qualcosa che non ne ha; poi ci fa credere che queste macchine siano inutili.

Nel febbraio 2023 lo scrittore Ted Chiang ha paragonato ChatGpt, che era diventato pubblico da poco, a un jpeg sfocato del web . Cioè, un’immagine compressa, con una perdita di dettagli, che però conserva un’impressione di visione d’insieme. È una metafora efficace per spiegare perché le risposte delle ia sembrano giuste anche quando sono approssimative.

Il rischio è che ci faccia pensare che le ia siano degli hard disk , dei contenitori di copie più o meno sbiadite delle opere originali. La conservazione integrale dei dati di addestramento, invece, è un’eccezione rispetto al funzionamento generale.

Non solo: come al solito in questa prospettiva la sfocatura è considerata un difetto che mina alla base l’utilità degli strumenti. Invece esiste proprio perché le macchine non contengono i dati con cui sono state addestrate, ma solo una loro rappresentazione.

Secondo alcuni, l’uso delle intelligenze artificiali per alcune attività, come la scrittura, è paragonabile al doping. Questa metafora è stata rilanciata a proposito del romanzo di Thélyson Orélien . La parte buona di questo parallelismo è che ci obbliga a chiederci quali regole vogliamo: dove finisce l’aiuto lecito? Dove comincia quello che non tolleriamo?

Allo stesso tempo dobbiamo ammettere che quel confine sarà sempre una convenzione, proprio come le sostanze vietate nello sport. Il doping, però, presuppone un giudizio morale (chi si dopa sta barando). E presuppone anche che esista una prestazione pulita e naturale da proteggere. Ma la scrittura ha sempre avuto molte mani: editor, correttrici, traduttrici, revisori, come ci ha ricordato anche Claudia Durastanti.

L’analogia si porta dietro anche le sue istituzioni: il test, la squalifica, la lista delle sostanze proibite, la denuncia pubblica, le accuse anonime, il dubbio, lo stigma a priori. E la metafora del doping si concentra su chi ha barato ma lascia sempre fuori chi scrive le regole e chi può doparsi senza essere scoperto perché tanto ha già una posizione di privilegio.

La filosofa Shannon Vallor ha dedicato un libro del 2024, The Ai mirror , all’idea che questi sistemi ci restituiscano l’immagine dei nostri dati e dei nostri pregiudizi. È una metafora che abbiamo usato anche nella prefazione di Intelligenza artificiale , un libro curato da Internazionale.

Funziona perché, essendo addestrate con tutto quel che c’è di umano, le ia ci rispecchiano in tutto. Il limite, però, è la presunzione di innocenza dello specchio, oggetto passivo e neutro. Le ia sono costruite da poche aziende che scelgono dati, filtri, regole, comportamenti da premiare o da rigettare, domande a cui i modelli devono rifiutarsi di rispondere, limiti d’uso e prezzi.

Se le ia sono specchi, allora sono specchi deformanti, ma questo non viene detto a chi li usa. La metafora rischia di assolvere chi li produce, minimizzando il suo ruolo.

Ethan Mollick , docente alla Wharton school dell’università della Pennsylvania, negli Stati Uniti, suggerisce da tempo di trattare i chatbot come una persona, un collega o uno stagista da seguire. Come indicazione di metodo funziona bene perché, in effetti, si delega solo quel che si è deciso prima, si controlla ogni risposta e si pubblica solo quello che è stato revisionato e di cui ci si assume per intero la responsabilità.

Nello Cristianini, che insegna intelligenza artificiale all’università di Bath, nel Regno Unito, ha proposto di considerare queste macchine come “intelligenze aliene”. È una metafora efficace soprattutto perché ci permette di pensarle come strumenti diversi da noi, altri. Ma l’alieno ha il problema che poi finisce per essere visto come un’entità cattiva che vorrà dominarci.

Fin dal 2017 l’informatico Andrew Ng ha paragonato queste tecnologie all’elettricità . L’immagine dice qualcosa di vero sulla loro diffusione come infrastruttura, e insieme le fa sembrare ancora una volta inevitabili e neutre come un servizio pubblico per il bene comune.

“I dati sono il nuovo petrolio”, formula usata dal matematico Clive Humby nel 2006, è diventata, forse per puro caso o forse per un’intuizione straordinaria, l’analogia più precisa: estrazione, energia, acqua, territorio, potere sono tutte questioni che si intersecano nel mondo delle ia. A marzo del 2025 Henry Farrell, Alison Gopnik, Cosma Shalizi e James Evans hanno proposto di considerare i grandi modelli linguistici come tecnologie culturali e sociali , parenti strette della scrittura e della stampa, ma anche delle biblioteche, dei mercati e delle burocrazie.

Più o meno nello stesso periodo Arvind Narayanan e Sayash Kapoor hanno parlato di “ tecnologia normale ”. Queste sono le cornici argomentative più utili perché spostano lo sguardo da tutte le distrazioni da cui siamo bombardati alle istituzioni che organizzano la conoscenza e quindi ai ragionamenti sul potere. Anche in questo caso ci sono dei limiti: “normale” può diventare un modo per dirci che tutto sommato anche la concentrazione in poche mani è una cosa naturale. Le biblioteche che conosciamo, però, sono in gran parte pubbliche. Questa, forse, è la metafora più interessante di cui abbiamo bisogno.

L’ultima virata sulle parole da usare è quella di Trump, che ha deciso di chiamare questi strumenti “ superintelligenze ”, firmando addirittura un ordine esecutivo per abolire “intelligenze artificiali” da tutti i documenti ufficiali della sua amministrazione. È un favore alla Silicon valley che corre verso l’idea di una “singolarità”, cioè la creazione di una macchina che acquisisce coscienza e impara a migliorarsi da sola. È un favore anche alla paura e alla distopia e non fa altro che creare più confusione.

items.title: Digger è la miglior caricatura dei nostri tempi
items.summary: Il film del regista messicano Alejandro González Iñárritu è la rappresentazione perfetta del turbocapitalismo portato alla Casa Bianca da Donald Trump e Elon Musk. Con un incredibile e inatteso Tom Cruise Leggi
items.content:
Arriva in sala Digger , una grandissima opera del messicano Alejandro González Iñárritu – al suo nuovo film in lingua inglese dopo The revenant – con un incredibile e inatteso Tom Cruise. Come fare un film serio su una situazione, statunitense e mondiale, tanto grave, con una leadership politica a tal punto grottesca? E se si scegliesse la satira, come farla con un presidente così autocaricaturale come Donald Trump? La risposta è semplice. Con una satira e una narrazione lei stessa tutta scassata, e soprattutto un presidente e un governo ultracaricaturali, forse addirittura oltre la caricatura.

Tutto è oltre in Digger . Tutto è macilento, anchilosato. E anche quando non lo è, come nel caso dei pochi personaggi più giovani, è insulso a tal punto da essere preso a calci dagli stessi uomini ultracaricaturali. Tutto è vecchio, nel senso peggiore del termine. E la cosa investe addirittura il capitalista stesso, Digger, che dà il titolo al film con il suo nome ( digger è l’escavatore, qui usato per estrarre petrolio), interpretato da un grandioso Tom Cruise, irriconoscibile. Un’altra persona, un altro Tom Cruise.

Digger è un petroliere le cui estrazioni senza freni provocano un collasso nell’Artico, facendo staccare un gigantesco iceberg che per via delle correnti ha buone possibilità di schiantarsi sull’Europa, in particolare sui Paesi Bassi, generando onde gigantesche in grado di sommergere le città e provocare milioni di morti. Ma per Digger questo è l’ultimo dei problemi, essendo molto più interessato alla salute del suo gatto, peraltro anch’esso posticcio, quasi finto.

Iconicamente, Digger rimanda chiaramente all’immagine classica del petroliere con il suo completo e soprattutto la sua cravattina a cappio.

Il suo cognome, Rockwell, è invece un’allusione evidente ai Rockefeller, industriali, banchieri e petrolieri monopolisti. Il loro nome peraltro è storicamente associato a momenti molto drammatici e violenti della repressione antisindacale nei primi decenni del novecento, con il massacro di Ludlow durante la cosiddetta guerra del carbone in Colorado. Anche se per la verità già ci aveva pensato Carl Barks – l’uomo dei paperi Disney, come fu definito – a parodiarne il nome con un miliardario mangiacappelli sempre in competizione fallimentare con Paperone. Siamo da quelle parti.

E poi il presidente, interpretato da un grande John Goodman (come non ricordarlo, tra i tantissimi film, in Barton Fink dei fratelli Coen e in Matinée di Joe Dante, incentrato sulla crisi dei missili con Cuba?). Se ne infischia ancora più di Digger, l’Europa deve cavarsela da sola. L’antipatia di Trump per l’Europa c’è tutta, così come le sue ossessioni (che sono anche quelle di un po’ tutti gli ultimi presidenti statunitensi). In particolare la Cina che rischia “di farci il culo” e di allearsi con i russi. Ossessioni praticamente passate tutte in rassegna, velocemente, mediante battutacce continue: e qui è la gestualità e soprattutto la mimica facciale di Goodman a fare moltissimo, a trasmettere tutta la forza alle battute. E infine fa partecipare alle riunioni di governo il magnate, proprio come Trump, magnate lui stesso, aveva fatto con Elon Musk.

Eppure l’inizio sembrerebbe visivamente quasi paradisiaco. Il paesaggio che vediamo intorno alla villa del petroliere è pura pittura, evocativa. Merito del direttore della fotografia Emmanuel Lubezki, collaboratore abituale di Iñárritu. Insieme al regista è riuscito a districarsi tra l’uso delle miniature e del VistaVision, un sistema di riprese inaugurato nel 1954 come alternativa al CinemaScope, che già Paul Thomas Anderson aveva rilanciato l’anno scorso con Una battaglia dopo l’altra . Questa tecnica consente di avere una grana dell’immagine più fine e dà più forza ai colori, oltre a maggiore nitidezza, integrando il tutto con i diorami realizzati dal berlinese Simon Weisse.

Ma se ci soffermiamo su questo è anche perché il film cerca, quasi ideologicamente, di suscitare nello spettatore un sentimento di bellezza usando quanto c’è di bello nel vecchio, in contrapposizione con la bruttezza del mondo vecchio e ricco rappresentato. E perché facendo percepire al meglio la dimensione totalmente instabile del film, sia narrativa sia visiva, si metaforizza l’instabilità totale del mondo reale, sempre più irreale, in cui si passa dalla satira al dramma, dalla farsa alla tragedia, come avviene, addirittura rivendicato, anche in Digger .

A ben guardare il film si rivela come nient’altro che un gigantesco set teatrale (seconda incursione di Iñárritu nel teatro, dopo Birdman ), in cui Cruise è anche Curtis Markson, attore protagonista di Fossil fools , una gigantesca e spettacolare pièce teatrale dove interpreta il petroliere Digger Rockwell. In altre parole Cruise interpreta due personaggi per due livelli narrativi, uno per la pièce e uno per quella che sarebbe la realtà. Una pièce che fin dal titolo (stupidi fossili) dice molto e che ha l’intento di rievocare quanto successo decenni prima in un pianeta ormai abituatosi insanamente a vivere semisommerso nelle acque: attitudine cieca che è in realtà una fotografia critica del nostro modo di stare al mondo più che una proiezione del futuro.

Ma c’è un’ombra pesante anche su chi tiene le fila della pièce, cioè della finzione: il produttore nascosto è il figlio di Rockwell, che ha un suo servizio di sicurezza privato, usato per ritrovare la figlia di Markson. Sappiamo che la donna è a bordo di un volo, ma di lei non si hanno notizie (altro riferimento a Musk, e alla sua Starlink).

Il film-teatro in verità mette il dito su una questione centrale, l’esaurimento delle risorse del pianeta, e su come regolarmente questo faccia impazzire il potere, tematica su cui molti studi e saggi recenti si sono concentrati, come per esempio, tra le uscite più recenti, La confisca del mondo. Storia del capitalismo della finitudine dello storico francese Arnaud Orain (Einaudi 2026).

Tutto in Digger è instabile e indefinito, tutti i mezzi d’espressione si confondono insieme alla realtà, alla finzione e alle scale di grandezza (i diorami sono dei modelli tridimensionali che ricreano una scena in scala ridotta). Dai vari livelli si scivola costantemente e senza soluzione di continuità, anche se il regista tiene magistralmente insieme gli equilibri, in realtà sottili, così come Cruise si mantiene in equilibrio perfetto tra la caricatura e il personaggio del miliardario machiavellico e manipolatore, che dice solo verità parziali, quelle comode per lui, contrariamente allo scienziato che lo sfida e che si sfinisce nel dire sempre la verità, anche etica.

In questa instabilità totale c’è la fotografia metaforica di un capitalismo impazzito, sempre più folle nella sua ubriacatura da vittoria sulla guerra fredda e perciò del tutto incapace di mettersi in discussione, di creare nuovi modelli, facendo così affondare tutti.

Digger è la miglior rappresentazione mai vista del turbocapitalismo portato alla Casa Bianca da Trump e Musk, e venduto alle masse come una liberazione. Perché in verità sono tutti delle turbocaricature.

items.title: The art of defusing a second world war bomb
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/06/it-could-knock-a-whole-street-down-the-art-of-defusing-a-second-world-war-bomb Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49987858 Points: 21 # Comments: 5
items.content:
On 14 January this year, army and navy squads faced an unprecedented challenge: one bomb on a Plymouth building site, another floating on a dredger in Exmouth. That afternoon, the clock started ticking

Everyone at Exmouth Marina knew there was an unexploded German bomb in the water. Old hands at the dock had been saying so since the end of the second world war. But the marina had been dredged and re-dredged and nothing had ever come up. It had started to sound like an old wives’ tale. The marina is a busy stretch of water: a commercial port until the late 1990s that had since been converted into a home to private yachts. A bomb, you’d think, would have a hard time staying hidden. But in the middle of the afternoon on Wednesday 14 January 2026, 81 years after the end of the second world war, Steve Hockings-Thompson, the manager of Exmouth Marina, got a call from the crew of a dredging vessel telling him he’d better come out to the boat. “I thought: ‘Oh crikey. We’ve got a bit of an issue here,’” Hockings-Thompson told me recently.

He went out to the dredger, a squat barge that hauls silt and other debris from the marina floor on to a flat deck that resembles a steel sieve. Sitting on the deck was a huge hunk of metal, caked in mud and stones. As Hockings-Thompson got closer and saw its distinctive conical shape, he knew it was a bomb – a big one. The dredger was loaded with 20,000 litres of diesel fuel, so if the bomb detonated, it would be disastrous. He called the police, who quickly came to the scene. “And then,” he said, “all hell broke loose.”

To deal with the explosives, they called in the army. The call was picked up at the control centre at Vauxhall Barracks in Didcot, a small town in Oxfordshire. This is the headquarters of the 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment (11EOD), a specialist army division responsible for all kinds of bomb disposal – from improvised devices planted by terrorist groups to second world war-era munitions.

When the Exmouth bomb was called in, Maj Andrew Boyce, who was managing operations for the regiment, was confused. “We were talking about ‘the bomb’, which I’d been told was a 50kg,” he recalled. “And then somebody on the phone tells me it’s a 250kg. I’m like, how have you confused a 50kg bomb, which is the size of a fire extinguisher, with a 250kg bomb, which is the size of a hot water tank?”

The reason for the confusion soon became clear: the Exmouth Marina bomb was not the first to be discovered that day. Another second world war bomb had been unearthed a few hours earlier at a building site in Plymouth, 50 miles away.

In Plymouth that morning, Luke Templeton, director of S.I UXO, a private contractor that goes in ahead of construction companies to look for unexploded bombs, had known what he was looking for. His company’s historians had already spent a fortnight doing a detailed risk assessment of the site, drawing on historical documents showing the Luftwaffe’s flight paths and local records of airstrikes. From this, they’d worked out that it was highly likely there were two bombs buried somewhere on the building site. Using specialist equipment, they had found a 50kg bomb buried more than four metres down. After inspecting the bomb up close, Templeton called the police.

As far as Boyce knew, this was the first time since the immediate postwar period that two unexploded bombs had been discovered on the same day. The two bombs were in the same part of the country, and had been reported to the same police force, Devon and Cornwall. “We’re used to having confusion with location or devices. We’re not used to having two devices,” said Brig Darren Fisher, who at the time was a colonel overseeing the operations. Once the confusion had been straightened out – it was a 50kg bomb at the building site in Plymouth, and a 250kg bomb floating on the dredger in Exmouth – the response began.

When most people think of bomb disposal, they imagine a lone figure in a bomb suit carefully approaching an improvised device as bullets fly overhead, holding steady as they unpick wires, knowing that one wrong move will kill them. This image was forged in Belfast during the Troubles and Helmand province during the invasion of Afghanistan, and it is not unwarranted; bomb disposal is commonly described as the most dangerous job in the military. But, in Britain in 2026, the daily reality of the job is quite different.

Although the same team deals with terrorist incidents, such as the 2017 Manchester attack on an Ariana Grande concert, it is unexploded second world war munitions that make up the core work of the UK’s bomb-disposal teams. The Luftwaffe dropped more than 60,000 tonnes of bombs on Britain over the course of the war, and the Ministry of Defence estimates that roughly one in 10 of these failed to explode on impact. The reasons range from the grim – poor manufacturing quality due to a reliance on forced labour in concentration camps – to the prosaic: a bomb might have landed at an odd angle, or on soft ground that absorbed the impact before the fuze could fire. (“Fuse” is the general spelling for electrical safety devices and burning cords, while “fuze” refers to engineered explosive detonators.) Britain also dropped munitions on its own land during training exercises and deliberately buried surplus after the war in an effort at disposal. Eight decades on, the physical remnants of the war still account for about 2,000 of the 2,500 incidents that military bomb-disposal teams respond to in an average year.

The calls often come in from metal detectorists and magnet fishers, hobbyists who throw strong magnets into waterways to see what comes up. They surge on bank holidays, when people are out walking and notice things underfoot, or catching up on tasks such as clearing out a grandparent’s home. Not long ago, the bomb-disposal unit was called to deal with a 2in mortar that had been used for 20 years as a paperweight. Increasingly, calls come from construction sites, as buildings get taller and companies dig deeper, which has led to a growing industry of private contractors actively searching for unexploded bombs. “We’re expanding cities, building new homes, and an accident could happen,” said Templeton. “If a 250kg bomb went off in a city, it could knock a whole street down.”

The passage of time has not rendered these explosives less dangerous. In June 2010, three bomb-disposal experts in Göttingen, Germany, were killed by a 500kg American bomb found beneath the site of a new sports arena. In 2020, a 250kg bomb exploded beneath a crab boat off the Norfolk coast , seriously injuring five of its seven crew. In 2021, another bomb exploded beneath a drilling rig near Munich’s main railway station, injuring four. Because it was a global war, this is a global problem. This year, a second world war bomb beneath a stilt house in Indonesia detonated, killing five people and injuring 20.

These decades-old devices are difficult to read or predict. “You don’t really know why [a particular bomb] didn’t function, which is part of the problem,” said Lt Col Andy Hambley, the commanding officer of 11EOD. Years of corrosion, shifting ground and rust make the fuzes less predictable, the machinery harder to read.

That was exactly the issue facing two teams in two different corners of Devon on the afternoon of 14 January.

At about 1pm, PO Scott Dooley, a diver and bomb-disposal operator with the Royal Navy’s Diving and Threat Exploitation Group, arrived at the building site in Plymouth. Dooley, a tall man with a neatly trimmed beard and a soft Devon accent, grew up in the military; his father was in the Royal Engineers, doing bomb disposal. In recent years, he had acquired the nickname “the Doom Watch”, because every time he was on duty, the phone didn’t stop ringing (his record was 11 call-outs in a single week). In Plymouth, Dooley scanned the area for risk: there was a school nearby, as well as a glass-fronted hotel that could shatter if the worst happened. Police were already at work establishing a cordon and evacuating the area around the bomb.

When an operator approaches a bomb for the first time, they do not know what they are walking towards. The most important thing is to assess the fuze, a metal cylinder screwed into the side of the bomb. It is the first link in a chain. The fuze contains explosives, which fire a tiny, highly sensitive detonator, which sets off a booster charge, which sets off the main filling of the bomb, a comparatively stable “secondary” explosive. Most German fuzes were electrical, charged from the aircraft as the bomb was released. After 80 years, there is no charge left in them. But some German bombs were fitted with a mechanical delayed-action fuze, constructed from gears and springs, like a watch. Once triggered, this fuze ticks down before detonating between two and 72 hours later. The Luftwaffe deliberately fitted these fuzes to maximise disruption; hospitals, roads and factories were cleared for days at a time because the bombs could detonate long after impact.
